origin_region: Yunnan · Xishuangbanna · Menghai · Xiding · Bada Shan
cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica); old Bulang village gardens plus extensive modern plantation
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried maocha pressed into cakes; plantation leaf from the mountain is a standard component of Menghai factory blends.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the old-garden lots; the plantations are picked spring, summer and autumn for factory use.
appearance_dry: Medium-large grey-green twisted leaves with white buds, pressed into a firm cake.
appearance_wet: Even, medium-thick yellow-green leaves, softer than Bulang material.
taste_profile: Light and fragrant for Menghai: flowers and honey, a mild clean bitterness, quick sweetness, a medium body and a fresh finish; the old Zhanglang gardens add depth and a longer aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Forgiving tea; standard steeps in porcelain. Factory-pressed Bada cakes are tight and want a slightly longer first infusion.

vintage_note: Sold two ways: by spring harvest year and village (Zhanglang above all) from boutique producers, and by production year as a named mountain in factory cakes from the big Menghai brand, whose Bada plantation base has supplied blends since the 1980s. Young (1–3 years) it is light and floral; it is pleasant in the 5–12-year window but is not a tea people cellar for decades, so aged Bada mostly means factory cakes. Supply is 2005–2025, dry-stored, and old-garden Zhanglang tea is priced well below Nannuo or Bulang gushu.
description:
Bada Shan is the mountain on the far west of Menghai County, up against the Myanmar border in Xiding township, and it is known for two very different things: the Bulang village of Zhanglang with its old gardens, and a large plantation base planted in the 1980s by the Menghai Tea Factory that has fed its blends ever since. The mountain was also home to a famous wild tea tree at Hesong, reckoned at about 1,700 years old, which fell in 2012.

The old gardens sit at roughly 1,500–2,000 m and are seed-grown trees under light forest; the plantations are dense terraced bushes. Both are processed as standard sheng, and the plantation leaf is pressed by the factory, while village leaf goes to boutique producers.

In the cup Bada is on the light side for Menghai: flowers and honey, a mild clean bitterness, quick sweetness, medium body and a fresh finish. Zhanglang old-garden tea adds thickness and a longer, cooler aftertaste. It is an easy tea to brew and a good one to learn on, because nothing about it punishes a mistake.

Sold by spring year and village from small producers, and by production year as a 'Bada' cake from the factory, which is a good and inexpensive way to taste the mountain. The village tea is modestly priced for genuine old trees; the thing to know is simply that most Bada leaf in the world is plantation tea in blends, and that the famous old tree was wild and has nothing to do with the tea you are drinking.

If you want to taste what Dayi blends are built from, a factory Bada cake alongside a 7542 of the same year is an instructive pair.
sources_note: The Bada wild tea tree at Hesong is usually quoted as about 1,700 years old; its collapse in 2012 was widely reported. The founding decade of the factory's Bada base is given as the 1980s in company history.
